name: Aisha Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can be as honest as you like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thank you for asking me. I will answer as honestly as I can.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I study chemical engineering, so my week is lectures in the morning, chemistry labs on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and problem sheets in the evenings. I live at home with my parents, Imran and Sana, and my grandmother, in a terraced house about forty minutes from campus by bus. My father is a hospital porter and my mother does clothing alterations at the kitchen table. I work Saturdays and two evenings at Dalton Pharmacy, mostly on the counter, and on Fridays I go to the youth group at our mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say that I'm not surprised, because a lot of loud promises are made about new machines. At the pharmacy, my manager Mr Dalton would say the same, that people still want a real person to talk to about their medicine. I would not post anything online, because I do not think it is my place to shout about what I cannot know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can carry on with my plan. I finish my degree, work hard and find a place in industry, perhaps at a water treatment company. What worries me is money, because I borrow for fees and my parents cannot help me at all. My grandmother's medicine is also a cost in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would carry on with my shifts at the pharmacy and ask Mr Dalton for more hours in the summer. I would apply for a placement year in a chemical plant, because experience matters more than words on paper. I would save a little every week, and I would not touch the AI tools, because I want to understand my work myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, on the whole. I feel the weight of money and of being the first in my family at university, but I feel steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want to understand your work yourself. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I solve a mass balance problem by hand, I know why the answer is right. If I let a machine do it, I might hand in a correct answer and not know why. My father always says that a tool you cannot understand will fail you when you most need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does being first in your family at university feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proud, and also heavy. My aunt asks about my grades every Eid and my parents tell people I will be an engineer. I do not want to let them down, so I work harder than I need to.

say: I'd say I'm not **surprised**, since loud promises are often made about new machines.
I would not post online about things I **cannot know**.
think: I can carry on with my plan: finish the degree and find a place in **industry**.
Money is the real weight, because my parents cannot help with **fees** and my grandmother's medicine costs.
do: Ask Mr Dalton for more **summer hours** at the pharmacy.
Apply for a **placement year** at a chemical plant.
Save a little every week and avoid AI tools.
feel: **Settled**, but aware of the weight of money and being first in my family at university.
S0.quote: A tool you cannot understand will fail you when you most need it.
fieldNote: Her calm is **steady** but money-shadowed: loans, her grandmother's medicine and no family help.
Refuses AI for a stated reason: wants to **understand** her own work.
Being first at university adds pride and pressure, and she works harder than needed.

steps.text: Ask Mr Dalton for extra summer hours at the pharmacy
Save a fixed amount from each wage every week
Apply for a placement year at a water treatment plant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say that change like this is normal, and that every generation has had new machines. But I would also say people should be honest about who loses out. At the pharmacy, Mr Dalton would say the stock ordering and the prescription checking will be done by software, and I would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the paperwork and checking jobs near the start of an engineering career will shrink, because they are the kind of tasks the software takes. The plant work, with pipes and valves and people on site, will change more slowly. So I believe a chemical engineer who can be at the plant has an advantage over someone who only sits at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the course and take the more practical modules, like process safety and plant design. I would still not use AI for my own work, but I would learn how my lecturers use it, because I do not want to be left behind completely. I would also ask my mosque's community network whether anyone knows engineers who would talk to me about their work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, somewhat. I do not like uncertainty, and I know my habits are slow to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools but you would learn how lecturers use them. Can you explain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching is not the same as using. I can sit in the lecture, see what the tool produces, and understand it without depending on it. It is a middle path, and I think it fits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible if graduate jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly the firms that choose the cheapest way, and partly people who expect help without effort. I believe the answer is training on the job, apprenticeships and families that support their children. I do not think a handout fixes anything.

say: I'd say change like this is **normal**, but people should be honest about who loses out.
I'd agree with Mr Dalton that stock ordering and **prescription checking** will move to software.
think: Paperwork and checking jobs at the start of an engineering career will **shrink**.
Plant work with pipes and valves changes more **slowly**, so being on site helps.
do: Take practical modules like **process safety** and plant design.
Watch how lecturers use AI without depending on it.
Ask my community network for engineers to talk to me.
feel: **Anxious**, somewhat, because I dislike uncertainty and I'm slow to change.
S1.quote: A chemical engineer who can be at the plant has an advantage over someone who only sits at a screen.
fieldNote: Traditional outlook shows in her answer: **training**, apprenticeships and family support rather than handouts.
Chooses the **plant-side** path because hands-on work changes slowly.
Middle path on AI: watch it, understand it, do not depend on it.

steps.text: Choose process safety and plant design modules next term
Watch how my lecturers use AI in design tasks
Ask my mosque's community network for engineers to meet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say that this is happening much too fast, and that nobody asked ordinary people. I would speak to the older people in my community and tell them to prepare, because they will need to understand what is coming. I would also say that families must stay close, because family is what protects you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my degree would be worth much less. I would graduate in 2029, with two years before the robots for plant work arrive. I did everything right, and the ground moved under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue with my degree, since a degree is still a degree, and I would take every extra shift I could. I would ask my parents whether we could cut our costs together, and I would ask my uncle who owns a small garage about hands-on work. And in the end I would use the AI tools too, though I would hate it, because refusing would not help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very worried. I would pray more, and I would feel frightened for my parents as well, because they have put so much into me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the tools though you hate it. What changed your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two years. If I had ten years I could resist for a while, but with two I cannot afford pride. It would be a decision made out of fear, not belief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would say, trust in God and work, and my mother would say stay close to home. They would both say that I must finish. They would not want me to see them worry.

say: I'd say it's much too **fast** and nobody asked ordinary people.
I'd tell my community that **family** must stay close, because family protects you.
think: My degree would be worth much less once I **graduate** in 2029.
I did everything right, and the **ground** moved under me.
do: Continue the degree and take every **extra shift** possible.
Ask my parents to cut household costs with me.
Use AI tools despite hating it, because refusing would not help.
feel: **Very worried**, praying more and frightened for my parents.
S2.quote: I did everything right, and the ground moved under me.
fieldNote: Her faith and family are her **anchor**, and she turns to them first.
Admits her AI stance would break out of **fear**, not belief.
Her worry includes her parents, who invested everything in her degree.

steps.text: Ask my uncle at the garage about hands-on work
Take every extra pharmacy shift and save the wages
Use an AI tool for problem sheets despite my dislike
Cut household costs with my parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say that five years is a fair amount of time, and that people should use it wisely. I would tell the youth group that we should help older people learn about technology, because those who understand it will protect those who do not. I would say very little at the pharmacy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I would graduate in 2029, and I would have a short time before plant work changes in 2034. If I find a place in a plant and gain good practical experience, I think I could make a life. It is not a guarantee, but it is a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a placement year in a plant, ideally one with older engineers who can teach me. I would learn to use AI tools in my second or third year, slowly, once I see which ones the plant uses. And I would save, and I would help my parents to pay off the small debts they carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Careful. Not afraid, and not comfortable either. I would say hopeful with a small knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would older engineers matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have seen many changes already. A person who has lived through a plant closing and a new plant opening gives you a way to think about this. I trust people who have been through hard times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What debts do your parents carry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loan for the house roof, and a payment on my father's old car. It is not large, but it is steady. If I earned well, I would want to clear it, because that is how I would thank them.

say: I'd say five years is a fair amount of time and people should use it **wisely**.
I'd tell the youth group to help older people learn about **technology**.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with a short time before **plant work** changes in 2034.
A place in a plant and good experience could make a **life**, though it's no guarantee.
do: Take a **placement year** in a plant with older engineers.
Learn AI tools slowly in second or third year.
Save, and help my parents clear their **small debts**.
feel: **Careful**, hopeful, with a small knot in my stomach.
S3.quote: I trust people who have been through hard times.
fieldNote: Five years lets her trust in **experience** shape the plan: older engineers as teachers.
Wants to clear her parents' small **debts** as a way of thanking them.
Community-minded: wants to help older people understand technology.

steps.text: Apply for a placement year at a plant with senior engineers
Learn the AI tools the plant actually uses
Save a share of each wage for my parents' roof loan
Run a technology help session for older people at the youth group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say that ten years is time enough to prepare properly, and that no one should panic. I would tell friends to finish their degrees, work hard and stay close to family. I would say the same at home, over dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years means I could finish the degree and spend a few years in a plant, and perhaps start a family. The big change would still come, but I would be a little older and more settled. I would be less afraid of it than of the two-year picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would complete the degree and the placement, and I would learn the AI tools in the later years, when they are more reliable. I would save for a small deposit on a flat, and I would keep helping at the pharmacy until I graduate. And I would keep attending the youth group, because the people there are my network.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, mostly. I would still be careful with money, but I could plan my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might start a family in this picture. How does that fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In our community, marriage and family are not something I put aside for work. With ten years, I could do both in a sensible order. With two years, I would have to put everything on hold, and I would resent that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Working as a process engineer in a plant near home, married, with my grandmother's house kept in the family. A quiet life, with a good job and my people close.

say: I'd say ten years is time enough to prepare, and **no one** should panic.
I'd tell friends to finish their degrees and stay close to **family**.
think: I could finish the degree, spend a few years in a plant and perhaps start a **family**.
The change would come, but I'd be older and more **settled**.
do: Complete the degree and **placement**, then learn AI tools in later years.
Save for a small deposit on a flat.
Keep attending the youth group, because that is my **network**.
feel: **Peaceful**, mostly; I could plan my life.
S4.quote: In our community, marriage and family are not something I put aside for work.
fieldNote: Ten years allows her to order her life in a **traditional** sequence: degree, plant, then marriage.
Network is community-based: the youth group and **mosque**, not online groups.
Her picture of success is modest: a process engineering job near home.

steps.text: Complete the degree and the plant placement as planned
Save for a deposit on a small flat
Plan my marriage and work in a sensible order
Learn the plant's AI tools once they are reliable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is not enough for me, my parents or my community to prepare, and my degree would be worth less just as I finish it. What would help is practical training on the job, apprenticeships that lead to real work, and a community that checks on its older people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being the first in the family at university makes every worry heavier. I carry my parents' hopes, and that is a good weight, but it is a weight.

headlineQuote: I carry my parents' hopes, and that is a good weight, but it is a weight.
portrait: **Aisha** is an eighteen-year-old chemical engineering student, the first in her family at university, who works at a pharmacy counter.
She lives with her parents and grandmother, relies on faith and **community**, and refuses AI tools to understand her work herself.
Her traditional outlook favours training, apprenticeships and family support over **handouts**.
Two years make her anxious and fearful for her parents; ten years let her plan work, marriage and savings in order.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because two years is not enough for her, her parents or her community to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Practical **training** on the job, apprenticeships that lead to real work, and a community that checks on older people.
